title: AI Meeting Assistants in 2026: Stop Paying Twice
body_md:
I'll verify the current pricing and feature claims before rewriting.

![fireflies.ai official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/ai-meeting-assistants-in-2026-stop-paying-twice/1.png)
*Screenshot of fireflies.ai ([source](https://fireflies.ai/pricing))*

**My verdict:** If you're already paying for Zoom, Google Workspace, or Microsoft 365, a separate AI meeting assistant is probably a duplicate bill — check what's already switched on in your account before you buy anything. The standalone tools earn their money in one specific situation: you hop between platforms (a Zoom call, then a Google Meet, then a client's Teams link) and you need every one of those in a single searchable archive. I'm leading with that because the buying question here isn't "is AI note-taking good yet" — it mostly is — it's "am I about to pay $8–20 a seat for something my employer already bought."

## What's Actually Going On

![guide.fireflies.ai official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/ai-meeting-assistants-in-2026-stop-paying-twice/2.png)
*Screenshot of guide.fireflies.ai ([source](https://guide.fireflies.ai/articles/3734844560-learn-about-the-fireflies-pricing-plans))*

An AI meeting assistant does roughly four things: joins or records the call, transcribes it, writes a summary, and pulls out action items. Some also let you search across every meeting you've ever had, which is the feature people underrate.

There are two flavors, and they're priced completely differently.

**Built into the platform.** Zoom folded its AI Companion into paid accounts at no additional cost, which it announced on September 5, 2023 — notable at the time because the rest of the industry was charging a per-seat AI surcharge. Zoom spread it across Meetings, Team Chat, Phone, Email, and Whiteboard. Google and Microsoft have their own equivalents inside Workspace and Teams.

Two things have changed since that announcement, and both cut against the clean "it's free" story. Zoom now also sells a standalone AI Companion at $10 per user per month that doesn't require a Workplace license, and its agentic product, ZoomMate, launched June 1, 2026 starting at $20 per user per month. The bundled core — summaries, action items, transcripts — is still bundled. The newest marketing is not.

The other catch: your admin controls whether it's on, and you need a paid license, not the free tier.

**Standalone bots.** Fireflies, Otter, Fathom and friends. These join your calendar invites as a participant, so they work the same whether the meeting is on Zoom, Meet, or Teams. Fireflies lists a free tier, Pro at $10 per user per month billed annually or $18 billed monthly, Business at $19 annually or $29 monthly, and Enterprise at $39 per user annually. Pro includes unlimited transcription, 8,000 minutes of storage per seat, AI summaries, and all integrations, with AI credits metered at 20 a month on Free and Pro, 30 on Business, 50 on Enterprise.

That "AI credits" line is the part worth staring at. Transcription is unlimited; the fancier AI actions are metered. Read any vendor's credit definition carefully before assuming "unlimited" covers what you want to do.

Otter is the other name everyone brings up, and its pricing is gated by minutes rather than credits. Pricing trackers checking Otter's page in October 2026 list Basic free with 300 minutes a month, Pro at $8.33 per user per month billed annually or $16.99 monthly with 1,200 minutes, Business at $19.99 annually or $30 monthly with unlimited minutes, and Enterprise with no public price. Basic cuts each conversation at 30 minutes, Pro at 90, Business at four hours. That per-meeting cap, not the monthly total, is what trips people up.

## Where It Breaks

![news.zoom.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/ai-meeting-assistants-in-2026-stop-paying-twice/3.png)
*Screenshot of news.zoom.com ([source](https://news.zoom.com/zoom-ai-companion/))*

- **Crosstalk and accents.** Transcripts degrade when three people talk at once or someone's on a bad connection. The summary then confidently paraphrases something nobody said.
- **It can't read the room.** An AI will record "team agreed to move the deadline" and miss that two people agreed through gritted teeth.
- **Action items get attributed to the wrong person.** Especially when someone says "yeah, I can take that" without naming themselves.
- **Metered features sneak up on you.** Storage caps, minute caps and credit pools — not the headline price — decide your real bill. Fireflies' Pro storage is 8,000 minutes per seat, which sounds huge until you're recording six hours a week for a year. Otter Pro cuts a single conversation at 90 minutes.
- **Bots in the participant list are socially weird.** A named bot joining a client call changes the tone of that call. Some clients will ask you to remove it.
- **Admin lockouts.** If you're on a company Workspace or Zoom account, IT may have disabled AI features or blocked external bots entirely. That's not a bug you can fix from your side.

## The Consent Part (I'm Not a Lawyer)

Recording law in the US varies by state — some require only one party's consent, others require everyone's. I'm not a lawyer and this isn't legal advice, so check your own state and your employer's policy rather than taking a blog's word for it.

The practical rule I'd follow regardless of law: say out loud that it's recording, at the start, every time. Not because it's required everywhere, but because the trust cost of someone discovering a transcript later is far higher than the four seconds it takes to announce it.

One more thing to check: whether your vendor uses your meeting audio to train models, and whether that's on by default. This varies per vendor and per plan, and it's the single setting I'd look at before uploading anything sensitive.

## Built-In vs. Standalone, Quickly

| Comparison | Built into your platform | Standalone assistant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cost | Bundled with paid plans (Zoom includes AI Companion at no extra cost on paid accounts; newer add-on tiers are not) | Otter $8.33–$30/user/month, Fireflies $10–$39/user/month, depending on tier and billing |
| Works across Zoom + Meet + Teams | No | Yes |
| Shows up as a visible bot | No | Usually |
| Who controls it | Your IT admin | You |

## The Pricing Shift Worth Noticing

The conversation has moved from price per seat to price per unit of AI. Vendors advertise unlimited transcription while metering the part you actually wanted — 20 AI credits a month on Fireflies Pro, minute caps on Otter.

The annual-versus-monthly gap is the other trap. Fireflies Pro is $10 a month annually and $18 month-to-month — 80% more for the flexibility. Otter's gap is wider: $203.88 a year monthly versus $99.96 annually on Pro, a 51% difference. You're betting a year of usage against a coin-flip discount.

*Updated October 2026. This guide is based on vendor pricing pages and published pricing trackers checked in October 2026, not on a controlled side-by-side test of transcript accuracy.*

## My Take

I think a standalone subscription is a bad buy in 2026 for a solo freelancer or a small team living inside one platform. The built-in versions handle the 80% case — summary, action items, transcript — and you've already paid for them inside a plan you weren't going to cancel anyway.

The exception is real and I'd pay for it without hesitating: if you're an agency, recruiter, or consultant bouncing between four clients' meeting platforms, one searchable archive across all of them is worth $8–10 a seat, and no built-in tool gives you that.

My read on the Zoom story is that it's gotten more complicated in a way that deserves attention. Bundling AI at no extra cost was genuinely disruptive three years ago, and the standalone tools have spent that time competing against free. But the $10 standalone tier and the $20 ZoomMate layer tell you where this goes: the base gets commoditized, the new stuff gets a price tag. Assume whatever Zoom is advertising hardest next year costs extra.

Fair point for the other side: "already included" means nothing if your IT admin has it switched off, and plenty do. If you've checked and it's disabled with no appeal, the standalone tools aren't a duplicate bill — they're the only bill.

I'm not a lawyer, and the recording-consent question is the one place where guessing is expensive. Announce the recording out loud, check your state, and check whether your vendor trains on your audio before anything confidential goes through it.
